title: What I Think Could Be Challenging This School Year and How I Want to Respond
author: The Broken Copier
summary: Heading into year 15 of teaching, this AP Literature and English 10 teacher names three anticipated challenges for the coming school year, large class sizes of 180-190 students across six sections, the erosion of authentic writing feedback under pressure from AI tools and district writing guidance, and a personal loss of patience noticed emerging the previous year, and pairs each with a specific, proactive response rather than treating them as inevitable. For class size, the plan centers on protecting early-semester community-building time instead of defaulting to a stricter behavior-management posture, which the author argues becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy. On feedback, the response leans on collective feedback and guided self-assessment strategies that preserve authentic response to student writing while distributing some of the labor to students themselves. On patience, the plan is relational and reflective rather than technique-based: investing in building-level colleagues and practicing self-regulation before demanding it of students. The post closes with a broader, unresolved worry about eroding public confidence in public education itself.
points: The teacher explicitly rejects a behavior management lens for oversized classes, arguing that leading with control becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy for classroom culture, and commits instead to protecting early community-building time.

On AI and writing feedback, the post identifies three compounding pressures, district writing guidance, AI embedded directly in student writing platforms, and growing peer normalization of AI-generated feedback, as jointly eroding authentic response to student writing.
The essay is candid about a personal decline in patience, treating regulating oneself as a prerequisite for helping students regulate, quoting a colleague on noticing one's own dysregulation first.

The closing concern about eroding public commitment to public education itself frames the classroom-level challenges within a larger structural worry the author admits having no idea how to begin to respond to.
quotes: In a class of 25-28 students, if you ask me how Albert is doing? 100% of the time, I have a genuine answer I can give you. In a class of 30-33 students, however, if you ask me about Albert? I cannot guarantee that I'll have a genuine answer every single class period.

I think this instinct is understandable but also at least partially incorrect. In particular, I believe that if I go into the school year with a behavior management lens, then it will be self-fulfilling prophecy as far as the culture of the classroom that emerges in response.

To name some other challenges, all of which feel as if they are increasing: increased guidance from the district around writing assessments, increased embedding of AI tools into actual writing platforms that students use, increased norming of AI-generated feedback amongst teachers.

As Jennifer Haber wrote, before we can help students regulate, we have to notice when we're becoming dysregulated ourselves. This means being reflective not just on what I'm doing as a teacher but even more so how I'm doing.
My fear essentially is this: too many adults, including too many adults working in public schools, have decided that public schools aren't good enough for their own children.
There are consequences for not telling and sharing the good stories about what is happening in our schools, and I fear that we're only starting to see those consequences.
